traveler: Louis XVI, Louis-Auguste de France, duc de Berry, King of France and Navarre, then King of the French, then Louis Capet
title: The Locksmith King: from the Chapelle Royale to the Place de la Révolution
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Palace of Versailles: the birth of the duc de Berry
stops.campa: A boy is born at Versailles and given the courtesy title duc de Berry, a name for a child nobody expects to reign. He is the third son of the Dauphin Louis and Marie-Josèphe of Saxony, and the line to the throne of his grandfather Louis XV runs through his father and his elder brother before it reaches him. The court registers the birth and returns to its business. Within eleven years the brother and the father are both dead of consumption, and the short-sighted, methodical child who prefers maps and locks to conversation is heir to the oldest crown in Europe.
suggested_refs: The queen's wing of the Palace of Versailles, birth apartments of the royal children

stops.name: Château de Bellevue, Meudon: the sickly prince sent out of the court
stops.date_confidence: attested: French Wikipedia gives the stay as 17 May to 27 September 1756; the date here is the arrival
stops.campa: From the seventeenth of May to the twenty-seventh of September the duc de Berry and his elder brother the duc de Bourgogne are sent out of Versailles to the château de Bellevue above the Seine, on the advice of the Genevan physician Théodore Tronchin. The younger boy is delicate and the air of the court is held to be part of the reason. Bellevue was built for Madame de Pompadour. The royal children keep a summer in her gardens, four miles from the ceremony that measures out every hour of their father's day.
suggested_refs: The site of the château de Bellevue at Meudon, demolished after the Revolution

stops.name: Palace of Versailles: the third son becomes Dauphin
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date; the research pool places the death at Versailles, standard accounts at Fontainebleau, and the contradiction is left standing in the report
stops.campa: The Dauphin Louis dies of tuberculosis and his eleven-year-old son becomes Dauphin of France, direct heir to Louis XV. Fifteen months later the same disease takes his mother, Marie-Josèphe of Saxony. The boy is left to the duc de La Vauguyon and to a household of tutors who teach him Latin, history, English, and the arts of the mechanic, and who form him in the conviction that a king answers to God for a people he must never be seen to enjoy. He is devout, orphaned, slow of speech, and next in line.
suggested_refs: The tomb of the Dauphin Louis and Marie-Josèphe of Saxony in Sens cathedral

stops.name: Augustinerkirche, Vienna: married by proxy
stops.date_confidence: attested; the research pool's chronology lens dated this ceremony correctly but placed it at Versailles, which verification corrected to Vienna
stops.campa: In the Augustinian church in Vienna the fourteen-year-old Archduchess Maria Antonia of Austria is married to a bridegroom who is not in the building. A proxy stands for the fifteen-year-old Dauphin of France while the Habsburg court, which fought the Bourbons through most of the century, seals the alliance its chancellor has spent a decade building. She sets out for France within days. The Dauphin, at Versailles, has never seen her. The marriage that ends on two scaffolds twenty-three years apart begins with an empty place at the altar.
suggested_refs: The Augustinerkirche in Vienna, court parish church of the Habsburgs

stops.name: Forêt de Compiègne: the first meeting
stops.campa: The court rides out to the edge of the forest of Compiègne to meet the carriage coming from Strasbourg. The Dauphin sees his wife for the first time at the roadside, in the open, in front of the whole household: he is fifteen, awkward, and kisses her on the cheek because he has been told to. Louis XV, delighted with the girl, takes her arm. The party moves on to the château de Compiègne, where the Dauphine is received, and then turns south toward Versailles by way of the Carmel of Saint-Denis, where the king's daughter Madame Louise has taken the veil.
suggested_refs: The clearing at the edge of the forest of Compiègne where the meeting was staged, marked in later royal iconography

stops.name: Château de la Muette: the supper before the wedding
stops.campa: On the road to Versailles the party halts at the château de la Muette on the edge of the Bois de Boulogne for a family supper, and Marie Antoinette is presented to the royal family. Among the women at the table is Madame du Barry, the king's mistress, whose place there the Dauphine notices and does not forget: the quarrel between the two of them will run for years and be watched by every ambassador in France. The Dauphin says very little. The wedding is set for the following day in the chapel at Versailles.
suggested_refs: The château de la Muette at Passy, demolished in the nineteenth century

stops.name: Chapelle Royale, Versailles: the wedding
stops.campa: Louis-Auguste marries Marie Antoinette in the royal chapel before the assembled court, and the two crowns are joined in the persons of two children, aged fifteen and fourteen. A storm cancels the fireworks that evening. A fortnight later the postponed celebration is held in Paris on the Place Louis XV, where the crowd is funnelled between the building works and the carriages of the departing nobility and crushed against a ditch; something over a hundred people are trampled or suffocated. The square is the one on which he will be beheaded.
sources: The 30 May 1770 disaster on the Place Louis XV is standard historiography and is NOT in the verified research pool; flagged as an outside-pool addition in the report
suggested_refs: The Chapelle Royale of Versailles, consecrated 1710, site of the 1770 wedding

stops.name: Palace of Versailles: Louis XV dies of smallpox
stops.campa: Louis XV dies of smallpox in his bed at Versailles and the court turns in one movement toward the young man in the next room. Louis-Auguste is nineteen, three months short of twenty, and becomes King of France and Navarre. He inherits a treasury drained by his grandfather's wars and a magistracy his grandfather broke and exiled. The capital has learned to despise the crown it feeds. Within months he recalls the parlements, against the advice of ministers who tell him plainly that the monarchy will not survive them.
stops.quote: It may be considered politically unwise, but it seems to me to be the general wish and I want to be loved.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Louis XVI on his recall of the parlements, cited in Wikipedia's 'Louis XVI', footnote 29; the underlying primary citation was not traced in this research
suggested_refs: The death chamber of Louis XV in the king's apartment at Versailles

stops.name: Notre-Dame de Reims: the consecration
stops.campa: In the cathedral where the kings of France have been consecrated since Clovis, Louis XVI is anointed with oil from the Sainte Ampoule and crowned. He takes the coronation oath in its medieval form, including the clause binding him to drive heretics out of his lands, and afterward touches the sick for scrofula in the traditional way. The ceremony costs a fortune the finances cannot carry. Twelve years later the same king signs an edict giving Protestants a legal existence in France for the first time since his ancestor revoked the Edict of Nantes.
sources: The details of the coronation liturgy and the royal touch are standard historiography and are NOT in the verified research pool; flagged in the report
suggested_refs: The Sainte Ampoule of Reims, smashed in 1793 by a représentant en mission

stops.name: Paris: the treaty with the Americans
stops.date_confidence: year attested in the pool, which gives no month or day; defaulted to 1 January. The Treaty of Alliance was signed at Paris on 6 February 1778
stops.campa: France signs a treaty of alliance with the rebelling colonies of British America, and the most absolute monarchy in Europe goes to war on the side of a republic against a king. Louis XVI approves it as a matter of state: Britain humbled, the losses of the last war reversed. The war is won at Yorktown and it costs more than a billion livres, borrowed at interest, on a budget that was already out of balance. The officers come home with the vocabulary of rights. One of them, Lafayette, will draft the French declaration of them eleven years later.
suggested_refs: The Treaty of Alliance and the Treaty of Amity and Commerce, signed at Paris, February 1778

stops.name: Palace of Versailles: an heir at last
stops.campa: Marie Antoinette gives birth to a son, Louis-Joseph, Dauphin of France, seven years into the reign and three years after their first child Marie-Thérèse-Charlotte. The cannon of Versailles fire and Paris burns barrels in the street. The succession is secured and the queen, who has been mocked in print for a decade as the Austrian woman who cannot give France an heir, is briefly loved for it. The boy is frail from the beginning. He does not reach his eighth birthday, and he dies in the month the Estates-General becomes a National Assembly.
suggested_refs: The queen's bedchamber at Versailles, where royal births were witnessed by the court

stops.name: Château de Rambouillet: the hunting king buys a forest
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the pool gives no month or day, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: Louis XVI buys Rambouillet from his cousin the duc de Penthièvre and adds its forest to hunting grounds that already run from Fontainebleau to Compiègne to Marly. The court year is a circuit of these houses, autumn at Fontainebleau by fixed custom, and the king keeps the count of every animal killed in a book in his own hand. He reads English and works metal. He studies charts of coasts he will never see. The government of France is conducted around a man who would rather be in a forest, and everyone at Versailles knows it.
sources: The king's game book, locksmithing and English reading are standard characterization and are NOT itemized in the verified pool; flagged in the report
suggested_refs: The bergerie nationale at Rambouillet, whose merino flock outlived the monarchy that founded it

stops.name: Palace of Versailles: the second son and the last daughter
stops.campa: A second son is born at Versailles and titled duc de Normandie: Louis-Charles, a healthy child in a family that is already watching the elder one fail. In July of the following year a fourth child, Sophie-Hélène-Béatrix, is born; she dies eleven months later, in June 1787. Through the same two years the queen is tried in the public mind for a diamond necklace she never ordered and never received, and the affair of the necklace does what no pamphlet had managed on its own. It makes the monarchy ridiculous.
sources: The Affair of the Diamond Necklace is standard historiography and is NOT in the verified research pool; flagged in the report
suggested_refs: The trial of Cardinal de Rohan before the parlement of Paris, May 1786

stops.name: Digue de Cherbourg: the only journey into the provinces
stops.date_confidence: attested: the king witnessed the submersion of the ninth cone on 22 June 1786
stops.campa: The king travels to Cherbourg to watch the ninth of the great timber cones sunk into the roadstead, the foundation of a breakwater meant to give the navy a deep-water harbour facing England. He goes out among the works in a boat and is cheered along the whole road. He comes home moved by a reception Paris has never given him. It is the only journey into the provinces he makes as king. The same policy of rebuilding the armed forces has planted twelve military schools for the sons of poor nobles; one of them, at Brienne, has just finished with a Corsican boy named Buonaparte.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Louis XVI on the morning of his execution, 21 January 1793, of the naval expedition he had dispatched in 1785 and which was already lost; cited in Wikipedia, 'Louis XVI', footnote 46, primary citation not traced
suggested_refs: The digue du large at Cherbourg, begun 1783 by sunken timber cones

stops.name: Palace of Versailles: the Edict of Toleration
stops.campa: Louis XVI signs the Edict of Versailles, which gives non-Catholics in France a civil existence: the right to marry, to register a birth, to be buried, to hold property and follow a trade without abjuring. It grants no public worship and no public office. It ends a hundred and two years during which a Protestant marriage had no standing in law and the children of one were bastards by definition. The parlement of Paris registers it under protest. It is the most liberal act of the reign, and the last important thing he does that is entirely his own.
suggested_refs: The Edict of Versailles of November 1787, registered by the parlement of Paris in January 1788

stops.name: Palace of Versailles: the Estates-General convoked
stops.campa: The treasury suspends payments and the king convokes the Estates-General, the assembly of the three orders of the realm, for the following spring. It has not met since 1614 and nobody living has seen one. Necker is recalled to the finances; the deputies of the Third Estate are doubled in number without any decision on whether the orders will vote by head or by chamber, which is the only question that matters. Louis XVI signs the convocation as a fiscal expedient, to obtain a tax the magistrates have refused for two years to register.
stops.quote: must always consult public opinion; it is never wrong
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Louis XVI, cited in Wikipedia, 'Louis XVI', footnote 30; the fragment lacks an opening subject and verb in the source as quoted, and the primary citation was not traced
suggested_refs: The convocation letters of 8 August 1788 and the cahiers de doléances drawn up across France in the winter that followed

stops.name: Salle des Menus Plaisirs, Versailles: the Estates-General opens
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool's chronology lens gives 1 May, the date named in the convocation, while the body actually convened on 5 May, and the two lenses contradict each other
stops.campa: The deputies of the three orders process through Versailles and take their places in a hall built for the occasion beside the avenue de Paris. The clergy sit in violet, the nobility in black and gold with plumed hats, the Third Estate in plain black, seated last and furthest from the throne. The king reads a short speech on the deficit and Necker reads a long one, three hours of figures. Among the noble deputies is Lafayette, who will spend the summer drafting a declaration of the rights of man a corridor away from the king paying for the hall.
suggested_refs: The Hôtel des Menus Plaisirs at Versailles, where the Estates-General and then the National Assembly sat

stops.name: Château de Meudon: the Dauphin dies
stops.campa: The Dauphin Louis-Joseph dies at Meudon, seven years old, of a tuberculosis of the spine that has been bending his body out of shape for two years. His parents have watched it happen through the whole crisis of the convocation, riding out to him between sessions. A month into the Estates-General the king shuts himself away with the body of his son and will see nobody. Sixteen days later the deputies of the Third Estate take an oath on a tennis court not to separate until France has a constitution.
suggested_refs: The château neuf de Meudon, residence of the royal children

stops.name: Versailles, the tennis court: the oath
stops.campa: Locked out of their hall, which the king's workmen are refitting for a royal session, the deputies of the Third Estate walk through the rain to an indoor tennis court in the rue du Vieux-Versailles and swear, standing, with one dissenting voice, not to separate until they have given France a constitution. Bailly reads the oath and six hundred men repeat it. The king's answer three days later, annulling their decrees and ordering the orders to sit apart, is heard and disregarded. Sovereignty has changed address, four hundred metres from his bedroom.
suggested_refs: The Salle du Jeu de Paume at Versailles, kept as a museum of the oath since 1883

stops.name: Place de la Bastille, Paris: the fortress falls
stops.campa: A crowd hunting powder for the muskets it took that morning from the Invalides comes to the Bastille, and by evening the governor is dead and his head is on a pike. Seven prisoners are found inside. The fortress is worth nothing militarily and everything as a sign, and it is pulled down under contract within months. At Versailles the king is asleep when the news arrives and the duc de La Rochefoucauld-Liancourt wakes him. In Málaga that same month a boy called José de San Martín enlists as a cadet in the Spanish army.
stops.quote_source: Louis XVI to the duc de La Rochefoucauld-Liancourt, night of 14-15 July 1789, answered 'No sire, it is not a revolt; it is a revolution'; cited in Wikipedia, 'Storming of the Bastille', after Guy Chaussinand-Nogaret, La Bastille est prise (1988), p. 102
suggested_refs: The outline of the Bastille traced in paving stones on the modern Place de la Bastille

stops.name: Palais des Tuileries: brought to Paris
stops.date_confidence: attested: the march began on the morning of 5 October 1789 and the royal family was escorted to Paris at about one in the afternoon of 6 October
stops.campa: Thousands of women walk the twelve miles from Paris to Versailles in the rain over the price of bread, and Lafayette follows with the National Guard. By morning the crowd is inside the palace and two bodyguards are dead on the queen's staircase. At about one in the afternoon the royal family leaves Versailles in a carriage, escorted by guardsmen and by market women with loaves on their pikes, and is lodged that night in the Tuileries, a palace no king has lived in for a hundred years. No Bourbon sees Versailles again.
suggested_refs: The garden front of the Tuileries, burned by the Commune in 1871 and demolished in 1883

stops.name: Champ de Mars: the Fête de la Fédération
stops.campa: On the first anniversary of the Bastille, a vast crowd fills an amphitheatre that the citizens of Paris dug out of the Champ de Mars with their own hands in a fortnight. Talleyrand says mass at the altar of the fatherland. Lafayette, commander of the National Guard, climbs the steps and swears the civic oath for the federates of every department, and then the king swears from his chair to uphold the constitution the Assembly is still writing. The crowd cries long live the king and means it. It is the last day on which the Revolution and the monarchy are one thing.
sources: Standard historiography of the Fête de la Fédération
suggested_refs: The altar of the fatherland raised on the Champ de Mars, 14 July 1790

stops.name: Palais des Tuileries: the carriages blocked at Easter
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool's geography lens pinned this event at Saint-Cloud, which is where the family never arrived, and verification moved it to the Tuileries courtyard
stops.campa: The carriages stand in the courtyard to take the royal family to Saint-Cloud for Easter, where the king means to take communion from a priest who has refused the oath to the civil constitution of the clergy. A crowd fills the gates and will not let them through. Lafayette's guardsmen take the crowd's side against their own orders. The king sits in the carriage for the better part of two hours, refuses to have the way cleared by force, says he will not have blood shed for him, and goes back inside. Two months later he leaves this palace at night.
suggested_refs: The courtyard of the Tuileries, scene of the Easter blockade of 18 April 1791

stops.name: Palais des Tuileries: out by the unguarded door
stops.campa: Near midnight the children are woken and dressed. The king leaves his bedroom by a door into an empty apartment and walks out into the courtyard in a grey coat and a round hat, past guardsmen who do not look twice at a servant. The party gathers by ones and twos and takes a hired cab to the barrier, where a berline is waiting. Marie Antoinette loses her way in the streets and arrives half an hour late. They travel as the household of a Russian baroness named de Korff, and the king of France is her valet. They are behind time before they clear the gates.
sources: The Korff passport and the disguises are standard historiography, summarized in the pool only as 'in disguise'
suggested_refs: The Korff passport, issued by the Russian embassy in Paris, used to cross the barrier

stops.name: Fromentières: the king talks to peasants
stops.campa: The berline stops to change horses and the king gets out and talks to the country people standing about the coach. He is a heavy man in a plain coat asking after the harvest, and his face has been on every coin in their pockets since before some of them were born. Nobody knows him. The party is running hours behind and the escort waiting further east is counting every minute of it. Nothing happens at Fromentières. The recognition that undoes them is four relays ahead, and it comes from a man who has seen that face on paper money rather than on silver.
suggested_refs: The post road from Paris to Châlons through Fromentières, the route of the flight

stops.name: Chaintrix: the silver dishes
stops.campa: At the relay of Chaintrix the postmaster's family knows the travellers for what they are, serves them, and holds its tongue; the son-in-law of the house rides on the box to the next stage out of loyalty. Marie Antoinette leaves silver dishes behind as a gift, which is remembered afterward as the recklessness of people who cannot stop being royal for a single day. The berline goes on through Châlons, where townspeople recognize the party and applaud it in the street, and nobody stops it and nobody warns it.
suggested_refs: The relay house at Chaintrix-Bierges on the Châlons road

stops.name: Pont de Somme-Vesle: the hussars have gone
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool tagged this stop as reconstruction and placed it 8.5 km north of the real crossroads, both corrected in verification
stops.campa: The hussars of the duc de Choiseul were to be waiting at the crossroads of Pont-de-Somme-Vesle to take up the berline and pass it east along the chain of posts laid on by Bouillé. They have sat in a field most of the day. Peasants in the district, seeing cavalry standing about with nothing to do, decide the troops have come to collect a feudal due and begin to gather, and Choiseul pulls his men out rather than start a riot. The carriage rolls up to an empty crossroads in the evening and goes on into open country with no escort at all.
suggested_refs: The crossroads hamlet of Pont-de-Somme-Vesle on the Châlons to Sainte-Menehould road

stops.name: Sainte-Menehould: Drouet reads the assignat
stops.campa: The berline changes horses in the square at Sainte-Menehould, where the National Guard is already uneasy about the cavalry that has been posted along this road for two days with no explanation. Jean-Baptiste Drouet, the postmaster, looks at the man inside the coach and then at the assignat in his hand, with the king's head engraved on it in profile. He says nothing until the carriage has gone. Then he takes a horse, rides cross-country through the forest, reaches Varennes ahead of them, and has the bridge over the Aire blocked with a cart.
suggested_refs: The post house of Jean-Baptiste Drouet at Sainte-Menehould

stops.name: Varennes-en-Argonne: stopped at the grocer's house
stops.date_confidence: attested: the arrest was at about eleven at night on 21 June, and the return journey began on the morning of the 22nd
stops.campa: There is no post house in the upper town and the party loses half an hour hunting for the fresh horses waiting on the far bank. Drouet's cart is across the bridge. The travellers are taken into the house of Sauce, grocer and procureur of the commune, and by lamplight a judge who has seen the king at Versailles identifies him. The tocsin rings and the whole district turns out under arms. Montmédy and Bouillé's cavalry are fifty kilometres up the road. In the morning the carriage starts back toward Paris, and the journey takes four days.
suggested_refs: The site of the Sauce house at Varennes-en-Argonne, destroyed in the First World War

stops.name: Palais des Tuileries: the return in silence
stops.campa: The berline comes in through the Champs-Élysées in the evening, past a National Guard holding its muskets reversed and a crowd that has been told in placards that whoever cheers the king will be beaten and whoever insults him hanged. Something like two hundred thousand people watch in silence with their hats on their heads, which is the insult. The king is handed down from his carriage and walked into his palace as a prisoner. The Assembly suspends him, then, needing a king for the constitution it has almost finished, votes that he was abducted.
suggested_refs: The contemporary prints of the return from Varennes, 25 June 1791

stops.name: Paris: the oath to the Constitution
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool tagged this as unconfirmed and dated it to the bare month, where the constitution was completed on 3 September, accepted in writing on the 13th and sworn on the 14th
stops.campa: The Assembly finishes the constitution and sends it to the king, who accepts it in writing on the thirteenth and swears to it before the deputies on the fourteenth. He sits in a chair level with the president's and is styled king of the French rather than king of France. He keeps a suspensive veto, a civil list, and no army worth the name. In the same weeks he is writing to his brothers in emigration and to Vienna, calling the thing he has just sworn to a monstrous absurdity and asking the powers of Europe for an armed congress.
sources: The secret correspondence with the emigration and Vienna is standard historiography and is NOT itemized in the verified pool; flagged in the report
suggested_refs: The French Constitution of 3 September 1791, in force thirteen months

stops.name: Paris: war declared on Austria
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool tagged this as unconfirmed, which verification reversed
stops.campa: The king comes to the Assembly and proposes, in a flat voice, war on the king of Bohemia and Hungary. The Girondins want the war to expose him, the court wants the war to rescue him, and the chamber votes for it almost without opposition. The armies of the Revolution march into the Austrian Netherlands and break at first contact, and Paris starts looking for the traitor who arranged it. In garrison that year a royal artillery officer named Paul Barbier lays down his commission, a nobleman in the king's uniform at the moment that becomes a sentence.
suggested_refs: The declaration of war of 20 April 1792, addressed to the king of Bohemia and Hungary rather than to the Emperor

stops.name: Palais des Tuileries: the tenth of August
stops.campa: At dawn the sections of Paris and the fédérés from Marseille and Brest march on the Tuileries. The royal family crosses the garden on foot in the early light and takes refuge in the reporters' box of the Assembly, in the riding school next door, where it sits through the whole day. In the palace the Swiss Guards are firing, and the king writes out an order in his own hand for them to ground their arms and withdraw to barracks. They obey and are killed in the courtyards, on the stairs, and in the streets they retreat through. The monarchy ends here, in writing.
suggested_refs: The Lion of Lucerne, carved in 1821 for the Swiss Guards killed on 10 August 1792

stops.name: Tour du Temple: the tower
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool's chronology lens gave only '1792-08' while its geography lens gave the exact date
stops.campa: After three days in a convent cell behind the Assembly, the family is driven across Paris to the Temple, the old fortified enclosure of the Knights Templar, and lodged in the medieval tower: four floors, a spiral stair, walls three metres thick, shutters angled so that the windows show nothing but sky. The king is separated from the others at the end of September. He teaches his son Latin and geography in the mornings, reads Hume on the Stuarts in the afternoons, and is walked in the garden by municipal officers who keep their hats on.
sources: The Hume reading and the daily routine in the tower are standard historiography, from Cléry's journal, and are NOT in the verified pool; flagged in the report
suggested_refs: Jean-Baptiste Cléry, Journal de ce qui s'est passé à la Tour du Temple (1798)

stops.name: Paris: the monarchy abolished
stops.campa: On its first working day the National Convention, elected by universal male suffrage while the prisons of Paris were being emptied by massacre, abolishes royalty in France. The vote is taken by acclamation, without debate, in a few minutes. The next day the Republic is dated year one. In the tower the prisoner is told that he is no longer king and is to be called Louis Capet, after a surname his family has not used in eight hundred years and never legally bore. He corrects the officers on the point and then answers to it.
suggested_refs: The decree of 21 September 1792 abolishing royalty, and the dating of year one from 22 September

stops.name: Salle du Manège: the interrogation
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool fused the 4 December indictment with the interrogation, which verification separated to 11 December
stops.campa: The Convention has argued for a month over whether a king can be tried at all. Saint-Just says he cannot be judged and must simply be killed as an enemy; Robespierre says the Revolution is itself the verdict; the Girondins insist on a trial. On the third of December the Convention votes to try him, on the fourth the indictment is read, on the sixth it decrees the form. On the eleventh Louis Capet is brought from the Temple through streets lined with troops and questioned on thirty-three counts, standing, without counsel, and denies almost all of them.
suggested_refs: The Salle du Manège in the Tuileries gardens, seat of the Assembly and then the Convention

stops.name: Salle du Manège: de Sèze speaks for the defense
stops.campa: Raymond de Sèze speaks for three hours at the bar with Malesherbes and Tronchet beside him. Malesherbes is seventy-one, was the king's minister, volunteered for this, and will go to the guillotine himself in 1794 with his daughter and his grandchildren. De Sèze argues that the constitution these same deputies wrote declared the king inviolable, and that they have made themselves accuser, jury, and judge in one chamber and are looking for a verdict they reached before the trial opened. The Convention hears him to the end and orders the vote.
stops.quote: I pardon those who have become my enemies, and I pray God to pardon them in the same manner.
stops.quote_source: Last Will and Testament of Louis XVI, dictated in the Temple on 25 December 1792, the day before the defense was heard; printed in 'The Trial of Louis XVI, Late King of France, Who Was Beheaded on Monday, January 21, 1793', Part 3 (English translation, Wikisource)
sources: The 1794 execution of Malesherbes is standard historiography and is NOT in the verified pool; flagged in the report
suggested_refs: Raymond de Sèze, Défense de Louis, printed in Paris in 1792

stops.name: Salle du Manège: guilty, by six hundred and eighty-three voices
stops.campa: The deputies vote from the tribune, one at a time, by name, aloud, each answer written down and printed in the morning papers. On the question whether Louis Capet is guilty of conspiracy against liberty and the safety of the state, six hundred and eighty-three vote yes and not one votes no. On the question whether the judgment should be referred to the people for ratification, the Convention votes no. Eleven days earlier, across the river, Haüy and Lavoisier had been weighing water together to fix the new measures of the Republic.
stops.quote: I protest, that I am not guilty of any of the crimes, with which I am reproached.
stops.quote_source: Last Will and Testament of Louis XVI, dictated 25 December 1792, printed in 'The Trial of Louis XVI, Late King of France, Who Was Beheaded on Monday, January 21, 1793', Part 3 (English translation, Wikisource)
suggested_refs: The printed roll-call of the Convention's votes, sold in Paris the following morning

stops.name: Salle du Manège: death, by a majority of one
stops.date_confidence: attested: the roll call on the penalty ran through 16-17 January and death was proclaimed in the early hours of the 17th; the pool's chronology lens misdated this to 20 January, which is the day the reprieve was refused
stops.campa: The roll call on the penalty begins on the sixteenth and runs all night, twenty-four hours of deputies climbing to the tribune to say one word in front of the galleries. The king's cousin the duc d'Orléans, sitting as Philippe Égalité, votes death. In the small hours of the seventeenth the president reads the count: three hundred and sixty-one voices for death without condition out of seven hundred and twenty-one cast, a majority of one. On the twentieth the Convention refuses a reprieve, three hundred and eighty against three hundred and ten.
suggested_refs: The register of the appel nominal of 16-17 January 1793, deputy by deputy

stops.name: Tour du Temple: the reprieve refused, the farewell
stops.campa: A delegation of the Convention climbs to the tower in the evening and reads him the decree: guilty, death, no reprieve, execution within twenty-four hours. He asks for three days, a confessor, and his family, and is given the confessor and the family. At half past eight his wife, his sister, his daughter, and his son are brought down and stay nearly two hours, the dining-room door left open and the guards watching through the glass. They arrange to come again in the morning. He does not send for them. His knife is taken away from him that night.
stops.quote_source: Louis XVI in his chamber after the final family visit, 20-21 January 1793, in 'The Trial of Louis XVI, Late King of France, Who Was Beheaded on Monday, January 21, 1793', Part 2 (English translation, Wikisource); the pool cited Part 3, corrected on verification to Part 2
sources: Wikisource, 'The Trial of Louis XVI', Part 2
suggested_refs: The Tour du Temple, demolished by Napoleon in 1808 to prevent it becoming a royalist shrine

stops.name: Place de la Révolution: the execution
stops.date_confidence: attested; the hour, about 10:22 in the morning, is given in the pool's afterlife lens
stops.campa: He hears mass at six, gives Cléry his seal for his son and his ring for his wife, and does not send for his family again. The carriage takes two hours to cross Paris between double files of troops with the drums beating so that nothing can be heard. On the scaffold he refuses to have his hands bound until the abbé Edgeworth tells him to take it as a last likeness to Christ. He speaks to the crowd and Santerre orders the drums. The blade falls at about twenty past ten, the head is shown, and men come forward to dip handkerchiefs and pike points in the blood.
stops.quote: I die innocent of all the crimes laid to my charge; I Pardon those who have occasioned my death; and I pray to God that the blood you are going to shed may never be visited on France.
stops.quote_source: Henry Essex Edgeworth, Memoirs of the Abbé Edgeworth, containing his Narrative of the Last Hours of Louis XVI (London, 1815), as cited in Wikipedia, 'Execution of Louis XVI'; the executioner Sanson's letter of 20 February 1793 gives different words, and the report leaves the two versions standing
suggested_refs: The Place de la Concorde, which carries no marker naming the execution

stops.name: Tour du Temple: the death of the boy called Louis XVII
stops.campa: The boy the royalists call Louis XVII dies in the tower at ten years old, of tuberculosis and neglect, in a room whose door had been walled up to a hatch. He was taken from his mother in 1793 and handed to a cobbler to be raised a citizen, then left largely alone. A surgeon named Pelletan opens the body and steals the heart. In the two years between his father's death and his own, the same blade takes Lavoisier, and three generations of Noailles women in one cart, and misses Francisco de Miranda, who refused to leave his prison and outlived Robespierre.
suggested_refs: The common grave at the cemetery of Sainte-Marguerite, where the child's body was taken

stops.name: Basilica of Saint-Denis: the return of the bones
stops.campa: On the twenty-second anniversary of the execution, workmen dig in the old cemetery of the Madeleine and find under the quicklime a jawbone and bones that a commission is satisfied to call the king's, and beside them the queen's. They are carried in procession to Saint-Denis, where the Convention had emptied the royal tombs in 1793 and thrown a hundred and fifty-eight monarchs into two pits, and laid in the crypt. Marie-Thérèse, the daughter, the only one of the four children to reach adulthood, stands and watches it. Louis XVIII orders a monument, finished in 1816.
suggested_refs: The 1816 funerary monument of Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette in the basilica of Saint-Denis

stops.name: Chapelle expiatoire: the chapel of atonement
stops.date_confidence: inauguration year attested (1826); the pool gives no month or day, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: On the ground of the Madeleine cemetery, where the bodies went into the lime, Louis XVIII and his niece the duchesse d'Angoulême build a chapel of atonement: a Greek cross in cold neoclassical stone by Fontaine, three million livres, angels by Gérard in the half-dark. It is inaugurated in 1826, and a mass is said there every year on the Sunday nearest the twenty-first of January. A year after it opens Hegel walks the Louvre a mile away. The chapel is classified a historic monument in 1914.
suggested_refs: The Chapelle expiatoire, 29 rue Pasquier, Paris, classified monument historique in 1914

stops.name: Basilica of Saint-Denis: the heart is tested
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the pool gives no month or day, defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: The historian Philippe Delorme has the heart that Pelletan cut out of the child in the tower tested against hair cut from Marie Antoinette in her Austrian childhood and blood given by her living Habsburg descendants. The mitochondrial DNA matches. The boy who died in the Temple was the son of Louis XVI, and the hundred men who came forward after 1814 saying they were him, Naundorff buried at Delft under the name Louis XVII, Richemont, and the rest, were all of them liars or lunatics. The heart is placed in the crypt at Saint-Denis, near his father.
suggested_refs: The crystal urn holding the heart of Louis XVII in the crypt of Saint-Denis
